claims.target_lexeme: Snolly Goster ?< pejorative sn- / snoll(y)- + dialectal goster / gauster
claims.case_section: 4. Dialectal Ingredients and the Chronological Gap Before Snallygaster
claims.short_label: Dialectal 'goster' ('boisterous bragging') is a plausible ingredient in 1845 tall-talk compounding, not an established derivation
claims.statement: Northern British, Hiberno-English, and regional American dialectal goster / gauster ('boisterous bragging; to boast, bully, domineer', attested 1674–1829 in England, reprinted from the New Orleans Picayune in stylized stage-Irish dialogue in Georgetown, Ohio on November 16, 1841, and recorded in New Jersey in 1894 Dialect Notes) is a plausible second-element ingredient in 1845 'Snolly Goster' alongside expressive pejorative sn- or Scots/Ulster snool ~ snoll within Jacksonian four-syllable comic compounding, though no primary source directly links the elements.
claims.rationale: Dialectal goster matches the form and 'boisterous bragging' semantics of the 1845 ring-tailed-roarer boast, but because the 1841 Ohio token is a stylized New Orleans reprint and the first element snolly- lacks a direct witness, the derivation remains plausible rather than established.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Formal and semantic viability of British and regional American dialectal goster ('boisterous bragging; to boast, bully, domineer') as a plausible ingredient in a Jacksonian tall-talk compound.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Vernacular use of 'goster' by the 1845 Cincinnati performer (since CERT-3200-101 is a stylized New Orleans Picayune reprint) or a proven etymological link explaining how 'Snolly-' and 'Goster' were combined.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether the anonymous Fulton Institute author drew consciously on dialectal goster (and Scots/Ulster snool ~ snoll) or coined 'Snolly Goster' primarily through playful tall-talk sound symbolism.

limitations: CERT-3200-101 (Nov. 16, 1841 Georgetown, Ohio Democratic Standard) reprints stylized stage-Irish dialogue from the New Orleans Picayune and does not prove local Cincinnati vernacular use.
No pre-1845 British or American text records the compound *snollygoster or explicitly glosses its formation.
resolution_criteria: Discovery of the upstream 1845 Cincinnati Commercial text, a Fulton Institute manuscript/program, or contemporary 1840s commentary explicitly connecting 'Snolly Goster' to dialectal 'goster'.

evidence.reason: November 16, 1841 Georgetown, Ohio Democratic Standard (p. 1, col. 5) reprinting 'What do you mane by all this goster?' from the New Orleans Picayune in stylized dialogue.
evidence.witness_note: Demonstrates newspaper circulation, not Cincinnati vernacular speech.

evidence.reason: John Ray (1674, p. 67) English dialect glossary entry 'To Goyſter: to be frolick and ramp, to laugh aloud'.
Francis Grose (1787, sig. E4v & *K3r) pairing North Country 'GAUSTER' with 'GOYSTER'.
William Carr (1828, Craven Vol. I, p. 177) 'GAUSTERING, Imperious, boasting'.
Joseph Hunter (1829, Hallamshire Glossary, p. 45) o-spelled 'GOSTER, to boast, to bully, to hector'.
Samuel Bamford (1854, South Lancashire, p. 181) 'Gáwster, to boast. Gáwsterin, swaggering'.
Francis Bazley Lee in Dialect Notes Vol. I, Part VII (1894, p. 331) recording New Jersey 'goster: to domineer. gosterer: one who boasts or brags'.
Joseph Wright, English Dialect Dictionary Vol. II (1900, pp. 579–580) synthesizing British and American 'GAUSTER / goster'.
John Jamieson, Scottish Dictionary Vol. II (1808, sig. 4X2r) documenting 'To SNOOL / snool'.
Joseph Wright, EDD Vol. V (1905, pp. 590, 592) attesting short-vowel 'SNÖLL, SNOLL' alongside 'SNOOL' with zero British *snollygoster.
Bartlett (1848, pp. 3, 68) documenting Jacksonian quadrisyllabic tall-talk coinages ('ABSQUATULATE', 'CATAWAMPTIOUSLY').
Farmer (1889, pp. 305, 502) documenting parallel American tall-talk formations ('HORNSWOGGLE', 'SOCDOLAGER, SOCKDOLAGER').
Establishes the 1845 Fulton Institute / Cincinnati Commercial tall-talk context in which 'Snolly Goster' first circulated.

claims.target_lexeme: snollygoster vs. 1909 Maryland Snallygaster and Berlin schnieke
claims.case_section: 4. Dialectal Ingredients and the Chronological Gap Before Snallygaster
claims.short_label: 64-year gap between 1845 'Snolly Goster' and 1909 'Snallygaster' weakens the monster-origin story without proving the reverse
claims.statement: The sixty-four-year chronological gap between 1845 'Snolly Goster' and the February 1909 Middletown Valley Register 'Snallygaster' stories—together with the twentieth-century date of Berlin slang schnieke—weakens deriving snollygoster from Maryland's monster name, without proving the reverse derivation of 1909 Snallygaster from snollygoster: the 1890 Judge poem explicitly identifies its 'snolly-goster men' as human White Caps vigilantes, neither the 1894 lecture spelling 'Snollygaster' nor Walt McDougall's 1903 fictional beast 'The Ticklish Snollygaster' is linked to the 1909 Maryland writers, and the August 1940 WPA Maryland Guide (p. 7) explicitly hedges its German 'schnellegeister' explanation rather than claiming to have invented it.
claims.rationale: Calibrating the claim strictly to dated attestations preserves the chronological argument against deriving 1845 snollygoster from a 1909 monster story while avoiding unproven claims about how the uninspected 1909 Middletown Valley Register stories were composed.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Sixty-four-year chronological priority of snollygoster (1845) over the 1909 Middletown Valley Register Snallygaster stories, genuine pre-1909 printings of '-gaster' in political and children's-fable contexts (1894, 1903), human White Caps identity in the 1890 'snolly-goster men' verse, hedged framing on p. 7 of the 1940 WPA Maryland Guide, and exclusion of twentieth-century Berlin schnieke.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: That the 1909 Maryland writers derived 'Snallygaster' from political 'snollygoster' (proposed by Blank & Puglia 2014 and Jack Daly, Contemporary Legend, 2026, without direct proof), or that the 1940 WPA guide's authors invented the German 'schnelle Geister / schnelle geeschter' explanation.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: What exact wording or etymological hints appear in the uninspected February–March 1909 Middletown Valley Register issues on Frederick County microfilm.

limitations: Original February–March 1909 Middletown Valley Register issues have not been inspected directly in this case.

Merriam-Webster cites an earlier January 25, 1890 Buffalo Morning Express printing of the 1890 White Caps verse (CERT-3200-403) and discusses Pennsylvania German 'schnelle geeschter', which already contains palatalized /ʃt/.

evidence.reason: October 9, 1879 Forest and Stream ([p. 703], col. 3) applying 'snolligoster' to an outsized forty-pound Florida redfish.

February 15, 1890 Judge (p. 313, col. 2, 'AN INDIANA HYMN.') identifying 'the snolly-goster men' in its refrain as human Indiana 'White Caps' vigilantes (earlier Jan. 25, 1890 Buffalo Morning Express printing cited by Merriam-Webster).
evidence.witness_note: Vigilante verse rather than supernatural abduction lore.

evidence.reason: November 29, 1894 Bellefonte Centre Democrat (p. 8, col. 3) printing 'The Snollygaster in Pollytics' fourteen years before 1909, without tying the spelling to the 1909 Maryland writers.
July 1903 Walt McDougall Rambillicus Book (p. 140) printing fictional beast 'The Ticklish Snollygaster', without tying the book to the 1909 Maryland writers.
1910 William T. Cox Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods (p. 15) southern swamp beast 'snoligoster'.
August 1940 WPA Maryland: A Guide to the Old Line State (p. 7; cf. p. 348) hedging that investigators believe snallygaster 'may well have been a corruption of the German schnellegeister'.
evidence.witness_note: Explicitly hedged attribution; does not state that the 1940 guide's authors invented the explanation.

evidence.reason: Merriam-Webster analysis noting snallygaster enters print decades after 1845 snollygoster while discussing Pennsylvania German 'schnelle geeschter'.
Establishes the 1845 print horizon of 'Snolly Goster' more than sixty years before the 1909 Maryland monster stories.
Supplies the bounded lexical checks across 1872–1924 Pennsylvania German and 1880–1899 German slang dictionaries.

claims.case_section: 4. Dialectal Ingredients and the Chronological Gap Before Snallygaster
claims.short_label: Zero lexicalized '*schnellegeischt' / '*schnellegeister' entries in four 1872–1924 Pa.-German works and zero 'schnieke' in 1880–1899 German dictionaries
claims.statement: Alphabetical and full-text checks across four 1872–1924 Pennsylvania German reference works (Haldeman 1872, Grumbine 1887, Horne 1896, and Lambert's 16,438-entry 1924 dictionary) find zero lexicalized compound entries for *schnellegeischt, *schnellegeeschter, *schnellegeister, or *snallygaster, and checks of Meyer's Der richtige Berliner (1880) and Kluge's Etymologisches Wörterbuch (1899) find zero entries for twentieth-century Berlin slang schnieke.
claims.rationale: Bounded dictionary checks confirm that no pre-1845 lexicalized compound is recorded in standard Pennsylvania German or nineteenth-century Berlin lexicons, while keeping lexical absence distinct from claims of phonological impossibility.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Absence of a recorded compound entry *schnellegeischt, *schnellegeeschter, *schnellegeister, or *snallygaster across Haldeman (1872), Grumbine (1887), Horne (1896), and Lambert (1924), and absence of schnieke in Meyer (1880) and Kluge (1899).
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: That an unrecorded compositional phrase such as Pennsylvania German 'schnelle geeschter' ('quick spirits', discussed by Merriam-Webster and already containing palatalized /ʃt/) could never have been spoken or adapted into the 1909 Maryland monster name.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Unindexed nineteenth- or early twentieth-century Pennsylvania German or western Maryland newspaper folklore outside Lambert's 1924 dictionary.

limitations: Haldeman (1872, p. 12) writes 'perhaps universally' for Pennsylvania German sp/st > schp/scht (citing verbal 'geescht' for gehest), and Merriam-Webster's discussed form 'schnelle geeschter' already reflects palatalized /ʃt/.
Absence of a dictionary compound in 1872–1924 word-lists does not by itself exclude ad hoc oral phrasing in western Maryland.
